question.text: A promoter of 'Narmada Developers' wants to raise INR 75 crore via structured private credit, using listed promoter shares as collateral, to avoid further equity dilution. Per Chapter 9, why is 'promoter financing' a legitimate private-credit use case for a Cat II debt AIF?

answer.text: Because SEBI mandates Cat II AIFs to fund promoters exclusively.
Because promoter financing is guaranteed by LIC.
Because Cat II AIFs receive RBI subsidies on promoter loans.

Because promoter financing lets founders retain a respectable stake (often targeted at ≥20% of paid-up capital) for management control and promoter status at IPO listing, while private credit fills a gap banks cannot.

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Chapter 9: 'Founders and promoters … have the challenge of retaining respectable stakes … usually desired at a level not below 20% of the paid-up capital of the company. Such stakes help them to retain management control and remain in the status of promoters when the company goes for listing. … In such cases, private credit can help promoters and start-up founders to shore up their stakes by promoter financing through structured debt.' **The Trap:** Options A, C, D invent regulatory or guarantee features. **Cross-Exam Context:** XV tests promoter-pledge economics. XIX-A covers the disclosure angle. XIX-C covered promoter financing as a strategy. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Cap LTV on promoter-share-backed loans at 30-40% (of 30-day VWAP) with automatic top-up if the share price drops 20%. Also negotiate board observer rights so the AIF has early visibility into promoter-level distress, before it becomes a default.
